turns.prompt_text: As a software engineer for many years I've used vs code. I've also used visual studio and a long time ago used notepad plus plus which I actually enjoyed for a while. I now kind of dislike visual studio code. It's nice but it's not as sturdy as I would like. It's a little rudimentary. I've also been fiddling with neovim and Vim and I really enjoy how sleek it is and quick. The problem I have there is that I can never find a good enough terminal for it. I use iterm 2 and it has a number of problems. The primary stopping problem is I cannot paste into it. The paste buffer is all screwed up and I've been debugging it. I've probably spent a few days just debugging it and I've come to the conclusion that it's not within my power to do
turns.response_html:
It is incredibly frustrating to hit a brick wall like that, especially when you're trying to build a sleek, distraction-free environment. Spending days fighting a paste buffer instead of writing code is a massive momentum killer.

The good news is that the terminal emulator landscape has evolved significantly over the last few years. If iTerm2 is giving you friction—especially with bracketed paste mode or clipboard syncing bugs that are notoriously painful to track down across the macOS clipboard and Vim registers—it is absolutely time to hop fence.

Here are the three best modern, rock-solid terminal emulators that pair beautifully with Neovim, each handling the clipboard flawlessly out of the box.

1. Alacritty (The No-Nonsense Speed Demon)

If your primary goal is raw speed and stability, Alacritty is a fantastic choice. It is a GPU-accelerated terminal emulator written in Rust that focuses strictly on performance.

  • Why it fits Neovim: It doesn't try to be a window manager or a multiplexer. It delegates all layout control to Neovim (or tmux), making it incredibly lightweight and sturdy.
  • The Clipboard Experience: It handles system clipboard pasting flawlessly via standard shortcuts (Cmd + V on macOS just works).
  • The Catch: It has no GUI configuration menu. Everything is configured via a single alacritty.toml file. If you enjoy configuring your IDE in Lua/Vimscript, you'll feel right at home here.

2. WezTerm (The Power User's Dream)

WezTerm is also GPU-accelerated and written in Rust, but it takes the opposite philosophy of Alacritty: it features a massive array of built-in features, including native multiplexing, tabs, and hyper-customizable keybindings.

  • Why it fits Neovim: It is configured entirely in Lua. Because the modern Neovim ecosystem is entirely Lua-driven, your terminal configuration and your text editor configuration will speak the exact same language.
  • The Clipboard Experience: It has robust, native handling of the macOS pasteboard and handles escape sequences for bracketed paste perfectly, bypassing the common bugs that plague older iTerm2 setups.
  • The Catch: Because it is so feature-rich, it has a slightly higher memory footprint than Alacritty, though it remains incredibly fast.

3. Kitty (The Feature-Rich Pragmatist)

Kitty is a highly performant, GPU-accelerated terminal written in C and Python. It strikes a great middle-ground between the minimalism of Alacritty and the heavy feature set of WezTerm.

  • Why it fits Neovim: It supports advanced graphics protocols (allowing you to actually render images inside the terminal if you use certain Neovim plugins) and has a very sophisticated keyboard protocol that handles complex key combinations perfectly.
  • The Clipboard Experience: Clipboard integration is seamless. It natively supports a feature called clipboard_control, giving you granular control over what can read and write to your system paste buffer.
  • The Catch: It uses its own custom tiling framework ("kittens") instead of traditional multiplexing, which has a small learning curve if you use tabs outside of Neovim.

A Quick Diagnostic Note on Neovim Pasting

Before you completely jump ship, there is a high probability that the root cause isn't entirely iTerm2's fault, but rather how Neovim is interacting with the macOS clipboard provider.

If you haven't already, ensure your system clipboard is explicitly linked in your Neovim configuration (init.lua or options.lua):

-- Sync clipboard between OS and Neovim
vim.o.clipboard = 'unnamedplus'

Additionally, macOS requires a clipboard tool for Neovim to pipe text correctly. Make sure you have pbcopy available (it should be native), or if you are running Neovim inside a container, SSH, or a specific shell environment, it might be failing to find the provider. You can check what Neovim thinks is happening by running:

:checkhealth provider

Look closely at the Clipboard section to see if it detects any errors.

If you're ready to abandon the iTerm2 headache entirely, spinning up Alacritty or WezTerm via Homebrew takes less than five minutes and will likely give you that sturdy, bulletproof foundation you're looking for.

turns.prompt_text: I'm going to try Allah Kitty. I am also familiar with tmux, however, I haven't used it much lately
turns.response_html:
Alacritty (or "Allah Kitty" as it may live in your heart now) paired with tmux is an absolute powerhouse combination for a Neovim workflow. It gives you the ultimate separation of concerns: Alacritty handles rendering at lightning speed, tmux handles window management and sessions, and Neovim handles the text.

Because Alacritty is intentionally minimal—it doesn't even support tabs natively—bringing tmux back into your rotation is the perfect move. It prevents your desktop from turning into a chaotic mess of individual terminal windows.

Here is a quick breakdown to get you up and running with a bulletproof setup.

1. Installation & The Setup

You can spin both up in a few seconds using Homebrew:

brew install alacritty tmux

Once installed, your workflow will look like this: you open Alacritty once, immediately drop into a tmux session, and run Neovim inside it. If your terminal emulator ever crashes or you accidentally close it, tmux keeps your session alive in the background. You just reopen Alacritty, attach to the session, and your exact cursor position and open files in Neovim are right where you left them.

2. Fixing the Clipboard in tmux

Since you just fought a massive battle with the paste buffer in iTerm2, we want to make absolutely sure tmux doesn't introduce a new clipboard headache.

By default, older versions of tmux used to isolate the bootstrap namespace on macOS, breaking pbcopy and pbpaste. In 2026, modern tmux handles this much better, but you still want to ensure your configuration is solid.

Create or open your ~/.tmux.conf file and add these essential lines:

# Ensure standard keys work for switching panes smoothly
set -g mouse on

# Fix terminal colors for Neovim inside tmux
set -g default-terminal "screen-256color"
set -as terminal-features ",xterm-256color:RGB"

# Focus events enabled for Neovim plugins that watch for file changes
set -g focus-events on

3. Quick Refresh: The 4 tmux Commands You Actually Need

If you're dusty on tmux, don't worry about memorizing the whole ecosystem. For a Neovim workflow, you really only need to know how to manage a couple of windows (which function exactly like browser tabs).

All tmux commands start with a prefix key. By default, it's Ctrl + b.

  • Create a new tab (window): Ctrl + b then c
  • Switch to the next tab: Ctrl + b then n
  • Switch to the previous tab: Ctrl + b then p
  • Rename a tab (e.g., "API", "Frontend", "Neovim"): Ctrl + b then ,

A classic setup is to have Window 0 dedicated entirely to Neovim running full-screen, and Window 1 dedicated to your build steps, local servers, or git commands.

A Smooth Transition Tip

When you open Alacritty for the first time, don't panic when it looks incredibly bare-bones or the font is tiny. It reads its configuration from ~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.toml.

If you want a sane starting point to make sure your text is highly readable, you can create that file and drop this in:

[font]
size = 14.0

[font.normal]
family = "Menlo" # Or your preferred Nerd Font for Neovim icons

[window]
padding = { x = 10, y = 10 }
dynamic_title = true

Fire up Alacritty, type tmux, open Neovim, and give the clipboard a test run. Let me know if Cmd + V or your Vim registers give you any lip this time!
